title: League of Women Voters of Greeley v. Board of County Commissioners of City of Weld
description: Whether home rule counties, like Weld, must comply with Colorado's redistricting statutes, with the plaintiff arguing they must comply and the defendant arguing they are exempt as a home rule county.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs, Weld County residents and organizations, argued that the Board of County Commissioners must comply with state redistricting statutes and sought an injunction to prevent the use of a non-compliant map.
defendant_argument: The defendant, the Board of County Commissioners of Weld County, argued that as a home rule county, it was not required to comply with the state's redistricting statutes when drawing new commissioner district maps.
decision_outcome: The court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, holding that home rule counties must comply with Colorado's redistricting statutes and ordered the Board to draw and approve a new, compliant map for the 2026 election.

title: Masterpiece Cakeshop v. Scardina
description: Whether the district court had the authority to hear Autumn Scardina's discrimination claim under the Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act (CADA) after the administrative process concluded without a final order on the merits.
plaintiff_argument: Scardina argued that she had exhausted her administrative remedies and that the Commission's closure order allowed her to file her discrimination claim anew in district court.
defendant_argument: Masterpiece Cakeshop, Inc. and Jack Phillips argued that Scardina failed to exhaust her administrative remedies and that the district court lacked the authority to hear her claim.
decision_outcome: The Colorado Supreme Court vacated the decisions of the lower courts and dismissed the case, ruling that the district court did not have the authority to hear Scardina's claim.

title: People v. Lopez
description: Whether a defendant who argues that his constitutional right to conflict-free counsel was violated by the simultaneous prosecution of defense counsel and defendant by the same prosecutor must prove that an actual conflict of interest adversely affected his representation, or if such a conflict, absent a valid waiver, requires automatic reversal.
plaintiff_argument: The People argued that the lower court erred by applying the Edebohls standard, and instead, the defendant must prove that an actual conflict of interest adversely affected his representation.
defendant_argument: Lopez argued that his constitutional right to conflict-free counsel was violated and that the Edebohls standard, which mandates reversal without showing prejudice for actual conflicts of interest, should apply.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the judgment of the division below and remanded the case to the trial court for findings in accordance with the standard that a defendant must show both a conflict of interest and an adverse effect resulting from that conflict.

title: People v. Lewis
description: Whether a county court, after finding a convicted defendant poses a danger to the community, can grant that defendant an appeal bond, or if existing statutes require both a stay of execution and an appeal bond.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the defendant posed a community safety risk and, under section 16-4-201.5(2)(a), an appeal bond was prohibited unless the court found the defendant was not a danger and unlikely to flee.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the county court erred by denying his appeal bond request, contending that his appeal was governed by section 16-2-114(6) and People v. Steen, which he claimed required the court to stay his sentence and grant an appeal bond.
decision_outcome: The supreme court held that a county court cannot grant an appeal bond to a convicted defendant found to pose a danger to an individual or the community, affirming the denial of the appeal bond while clarifying that a stay of execution pending appeal is still required upon request.

title: Sellers v. People
description: Whether a life without the possibility of parole (LWOP) sentence for felony murder is categorically unconstitutional or grossly disproportionate to the offense following the General Assembly's 2021 reclassification.
plaintiff_argument: Sellers argued that an LWOP sentence for felony murder is categorically unconstitutional or, alternatively, grossly disproportionate, especially in light of the General Assembly's 2021 reclassification of felony murder.
defendant_argument: The People implicitly argued that the LWOP sentence for felony murder is constitutional and not grossly disproportionate, even after the reclassification, particularly for offenses committed before the reclassification's effective date.
decision_outcome: The court concluded that a life without the possibility of parole (LWOP) sentence for felony murder for an adult offender is not categorically unconstitutional and was not grossly disproportionate to the offense, affirming the lower court's judgment.

title: Owens v. People
description: Whether the trial court committed reversible errors in jury selection, evidence admission, handling witness misconduct, and limiting impeachment evidence, thereby denying the defendant a fair trial.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the trial court properly conducted voir dire, correctly overruled Batson challenges, appropriately admitted evidence of prior shootings, rightly denied mistrial motions, and allowed sufficient cross-examination and impeachment, concluding that no individual or cumulative errors warranted reversal.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the trial court unconstitutionally erred by preventing voir dire on racial issues, improperly rejecting Batson challenges, abusing its discretion in admitting excessive evidence of prior shootings, erroneously refusing mistrials for witness outbursts and guilt declarations, and improperly excluding extrinsic impeachment evidence, all of which cumulatively denied him a fair trial.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of conviction, finding no reversible errors by the trial court.

title: Antero Treatment LLC v. Veolia Water Technologies
description: Whether the $25,000,000 supersedeas bond cap is unconstitutional due to separation of powers or equal protection violations, and whether the trial court abused its discretion by not ordering additional security or post-judgment discovery.
plaintiff_argument: Antero argued that the supersedeas bond cap is unconstitutional as it violates separation of powers and equal protection, and that the trial court abused its discretion by denying additional security and post-judgment discovery.
defendant_argument: Veolia argued that the supersedeas bond cap is constitutional, does not conflict with court rules, and that the trial court properly exercised its discretion regarding security and discovery.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the constitutionality of the $25,000,000 supersedeas bond cap and found that the trial court did not abuse its discretion in denying additional security or post-judgment discovery.

title: Colorado v. Seymour
description: Whether a "reverse keyword warrant" violates the Fourth Amendment of the United States Constitution and Article II, Section 7 of the Colorado Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The reverse-keyword warrant is constitutional, adequately particularized, and supported by probable cause, making the evidence obtained admissible.
defendant_argument: The reverse-keyword warrant is unconstitutional because it lacked particularity and individualized probable cause, thus the evidence should be suppressed.
decision_outcome: The court discharged the rule to show cause, affirming the trial court's denial of Seymour's motion to suppress evidence, thereby allowing the evidence obtained via the reverse-keyword warrant.

title: Aurora Public Schools. v. A.S.
description: Whether the Child Sexual Abuse Accountability Act (CSAAA) violates the Colorado constitutional prohibition on retrospective legislation by creating a new cause of action for sexual misconduct that predates the Act and for which previously available claims would be time-barred.
plaintiff_argument: The CSAAA is constitutional and should apply retroactively to allow victims to bring claims for child sexual abuse, even if previously time-barred, as it creates a new right for relief and serves public health and safety interests.
defendant_argument: The CSAAA is unconstitutionally retrospective because it creates new obligations and attaches new disabilities to past transactions by reviving time-barred claims, violating the Colorado Constitution's prohibition on retrospective legislation.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's order, holding that the CSAAA is unconstitutionally retrospective as applied to claims for sexual misconduct that predates the Act and for which previously available causes of action were time-barred.

title: People v. Smith
description: Whether a first-degree murder charge, after the legislative abolition of the death penalty, still constitutes a "capital offense" under the Colorado Constitution, thereby allowing for the denial of bail.
plaintiff_argument: The People argued that first-degree murder remains a "capital offense" based on classification, not penalty, citing prior precedent that defined a class of crimes permitting bail denial, and contended that the legislature's non-amendment of relevant statutes after abolishing the death penalty meant the exception still applied.
defendant_argument: Smith argued that he was entitled to bail because first-degree murder is no longer a "capital offense" since the death penalty, which defines such offenses, was repealed in Colorado, rendering the "capital offense" exception to the constitutional right to bail obsolete.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the district court abused its discretion by treating first-degree murder as a capital offense and denying bail, concluding that "capital offenses" unambiguously refer to offenses for which the death penalty is statutorily authorized, and the death penalty has been abolished for offenses charged after July 1, 2020.

title: People v. Platteel
description: Whether defense counsel may call an unsubpoenaed victim, who is present at a preliminary hearing, to testify, with the plaintiff arguing against it based on victim rights and the defendant arguing for it based on the right to call witnesses.
plaintiff_argument: Defense counsel may not call an unsubpoenaed victim to testify, as the Victim Rights Act (VRA) protects a victim's right to be present without being compelled to testify without a subpoena.
defendant_argument: Defense counsel may call an unsubpoenaed victim to testify if they are available in court and the prosecution's case relies heavily on hearsay, based on the precedent of McDonald.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that defense counsel may not call an unsubpoenaed victim who is in attendance at a preliminary hearing to the witness stand.

title: Woo v. El Paso County Sheriff's Office
description: Whether the Colorado Governmental Immunity Act's (CGIA) bar of a civil replevin action for lawfully seized property violates a defendant's constitutional right to procedural due process, given the availability of a post-sentence remedy in the criminal case.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, James Woo, argued that if the CGIA barred his civil replevin action, he would be left without a remedy, thereby violating his federal and state constitutional rights to procedural due process regarding the deprivation of his property.
defendant_argument: The defendants, El Paso County Sheriff's Office and Fourth Judicial District Attorney's Office, argued that the trial court lacked jurisdiction over the civil replevin action due to Woo's failure to comply with CGIA notice requirements and that any property return motion should be handled within the criminal case.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the court of appeals' judgment, holding that the CGIA's bar of Woo's civil replevin action does not render the CGIA unconstitutional because Woo has an adequate post-sentence remedy in his criminal case to seek the return of lawfully seized property.

title: Fine v. Ward (In re Titles)
description: Whether three proposed initiatives, which include provisions to allow food retailers to sell wine and authorize third-party delivery services for alcohol, violate the single-subject requirement of the Colorado Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the proposed initiatives contain multiple subjects, specifically combining wine sales in grocery stores with third-party alcohol delivery, thereby violating the single-subject requirement of the Colorado Constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the initiatives' central focus is broadly "expanding the retail sale of alcohol beverages," and both provisions serve this single goal, making them sufficiently connected.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the initiatives violate the single-subject requirement of the Colorado Constitution because they combine two distinct and unrelated subjects, and therefore reversed the Title Board's actions to set titles for them.

title: In re Colorado Independent Congressional Redistricting Commission
description: Whether Article V, section 44.3(4)(b) of the Colorado Constitution creates additional protections against minority vote dilution beyond those provided by the Voting Rights Act.
plaintiff_argument: Opposers argued that section 44.3(4)(b) imposes separate and more expansive obligations to protect against minority vote dilution, beyond what the VRA demands, and that the Commission's plan impermissibly diluted Hispanic voters' electoral influence.
defendant_argument: The Commission argued that section 44.3(4)(b) merely incorporates existing protections against minority vote dilution as provided by section 2 of the VRA and expressed in U.S. Supreme Court case law at the time Amendment Y was adopted.
decision_outcome: The court approved the congressional redistricting plan, concluding that the Commission did not abuse its discretion in applying the substantive criteria of Article V, section 44.3, and that section 44.3(4)(b) does no more than incorporate existing VRA protections.

title: Francis v. Wegener
description: Whether Robert A. Francis should be permanently enjoined from proceeding pro se in any present or future litigation in Colorado state courts due to a history of vexatious and duplicative lawsuits, with Petitioners arguing for the injunction to prevent abuse of the judicial process and Francis arguing against it as an infringement on his right to access the courts.
plaintiff_argument: Francis argued that the requested injunction would infringe upon his constitutional right to access the courts and that his case was distinguishable from prior precedents used to justify such injunctions.
defendant_argument: The Petitioners (Benjamin Wegener et al.) argued that Francis had engaged in a decade-long pattern of frivolous, groundless, and vexatious pro se litigation, abusing the judicial process and straining judicial resources, thus warranting a permanent injunction.
decision_outcome: The court made the rule to show cause absolute, permanently enjoining Robert A. Francis from ever proceeding pro se as a proponent of a claim in any present or future litigation in the state courts of Colorado.

title: In re Interrogatories on Senate Bill 21-247 Submitted by the Colorado General Assembly
description: Whether the General Assembly can constitutionally direct the actions of independent redistricting commissions regarding census data use and dictate the judicial standard for reviewing compliance with redistricting provisions.
plaintiff_argument: The General Assembly argued that Senate Bill 21-247 was a well-intentioned effort to address census data delays and facilitate the redistricting process, filling gaps in the constitutional amendments without undermining the commissions' independence.
defendant_argument: The court argued that Amendments Y and Z created independent commissions, divesting the General Assembly of authority to direct their actions or define judicial standards, and that the judiciary alone defines its review standards.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the provisions of Senate Bill 21-247, which attempt to direct the independent redistricting commissions and define the judicial review standard, would be unconstitutional if enacted.

title: Poudre School District R-1  v. Stanczyk
description: Whether a school district is prohibited from asking or requiring a teacher who earned nonprobationary status in another district to waive portability of that status.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Patricia Stanczyk, and the Poudre Education Association argued that the relevant statute requires school districts to grant nonprobationary status to teachers who provide the necessary documentation, and that the Poudre School District violated Stanczyk's rights by requiring her to waive this portability as a condition of employment.
defendant_argument: The defendant, Poudre School District R-1, argued that the right to portability of nonprobationary status is waivable, that Stanczyk validly waived her right, and that the statute does not explicitly prohibit mandatory waivers. They also contended that enforcing portability would infringe on local control and negatively impact hiring experienced teachers.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of the court of appeals, holding that school districts may not require teachers to waive portability of nonprobationary status as a condition of employment, as such waivers are involuntary and invalid.

title: Markwell v. Cooke
description: Whether uploading a bill to multiple computers and using automated software to simultaneously give voice to different portions of the bill at a speed of about 650 words per minute complies with the reading requirement in article V, section 22 of the Colorado Constitution. The petitioners (Senate officials) argued that this method complied, while the respondents (Senators) argued it did not.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners, Cindi Markwell (Secretary of the Senate) and Leroy M. Garcia, Jr. (President of the Senate), argued that using multiple computers to simultaneously read different portions of a bill at a high speed complied with the constitutional reading requirement.
defendant_argument: The respondents, Senators John B. Cooke, Robert S. Gardner, and Chris Holbert, argued that the unintelligible computer sounds produced by the simultaneous reading did not comply with the constitutional requirement for a bill to be 'read at length'.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's determination that the unintelligible computer sounds did not fulfill the constitutional reading requirement, but reversed the part of the judgment that dictated the specific form or manner by which the legislature must comply with the reading requirement.
